\chapter{Asking Someone's Age}

\section[\ar{كم} \ar{عمرك؟}]{\ar{كم} \ar{عمرك؟} — asking age with a noun, not a verb}

\label{lesson:AR-C17-kam-umruka}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} You've seen Romance languages \textbf{have} their years, Germanic languages \textbf{be} their years, and Classical Latin itself use a third construction ("born" + accusative of duration). Arabic does something structurally different again: it doesn't use a verb for this at all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \ar{عمر} — life, lifetime, age}
\textbf{\ar{عمر}} (\emph{ʿumr}) = "\textbf{age, lifetime, life span}" — from the root \textbf{\ar{ع}-\ar{م}-\ar{ر}} (\emph{ʿ-m-r}), broadly tied to the idea of \textbf{living, dwelling, flourishing} (the same root behind the personal name \textbf{ʿUmar}, and words for "building, habitation"). Age in Arabic isn't something you \emph{have} or \emph{are} — it's expressed as a possessed \textbf{noun}: "\textbf{your} ʿumr," "\textbf{my} ʿumr."

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \ar{كم} \ar{عمرك؟} — no verb needed}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{كم} \ar{عمرك؟}} — "How old are you?" (to a man) — literally "\textbf{how much {[}is{]}}
\end{quote}

your\textbf{ \emph{ʿumr}." (\emph{kam ʿumruka?})}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{عمري} \ar{عشرون} \ar{سنة}.} — "I am twenty years old." — literally "\textbf{my} \emph{ʿumr}
\end{quote}

{[}is{]} twenty years." (\emph{ʿumrī ʿishrūna sana}.)

Notice there's \textbf{no verb "to be" at all} in the present tense here — Arabic simply juxtaposes two nouns ("my age" / "twenty years"), exactly the way it forms ordinary present-tense sentences without \emph{is/are}. So this is a genuinely \textbf{fourth shape} for the concept: not Romance's "I \textbf{have} twenty years," not Germanic's "I \textbf{am} twenty years {[}old{]}," not Latin's "\textbf{born} twenty years {[}so far{]}," but "\textbf{my age} {[}is{]} twenty years" — age as a possessed noun-quantity, stated without any verb at all.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "ʿumr" — age, lifetime, life span{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "kam ʿumruka?" — how old are you? (to a man){]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "ʿumrī ʿishrūna sana" — my age is twenty years, no verb at all{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \textbf{\ar{عمر}} literally mean, and what root is it from? ("\textbf{Age, lifetime}" — root \textbf{\ar{ع}-\ar{م}-\ar{ر}}, tied to living/flourishing.) Does Arabic use a verb to state age, the way Romance ("have"), Germanic ("be"), or Latin ("born" + duration) do? (\textbf{No} — it juxtaposes "my age" and the number, with no verb needed at all.) What does \textbf{\ar{كم} \ar{عمرك؟}} literally ask? ("\textbf{How much {[}is{]} your} \emph{ʿumr}?")
\end{tcolorbox}
